summary: Addresses problems with the SIP Record-Route header that proxies insert so later requests pass through them. It fixes issues with the URIs it contains.

eli5.summary: Proxies leave a note on the route so later calls come back through them. This repairs mistakes in how the note is written.

questions: what is double record-route in sip
sip record-route rewriting vs double record-routing
subtitle: Why SIP proxies that sit between two networks should record themselves twice, once for each side.

tldr.problem: A SIP proxy inserts a Record-Route header so later requests come back through it. When the proxy changes address, transport or URI scheme between its incoming and outgoing sides, one header cannot describe both sides, and implementations kept failing to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends double Record-Routing: the proxy inserts one Record-Route header for the input interface and a second for the output interface, so responses need no rewriting. It also gives rules for when to put a transport parameter in those URIs.
tldr.outcome: Double Record-Routing is the technique that SHOULD be used, while rewriting responses stays available as a MAY. The RFC adds no new protocol mechanism and clarifies how to use RFC 3261.

today: RFC 5658 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It changes no protocol mechanism, so it works alongside RFC 3261 as guidance for proxies and user agents.

sections.title: Why Record-Route Needed Fixing
sections.content:
A typical job of a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) proxy is to insert a Record-Route header into the first request of a dialog, so that later requests in that dialog pass through it. The header holds a SIP or SIPS URI saying where and how those later requests should be sent to reach the proxy.

At interoperability events such as SIPit, many implementations were found to have trouble with Record-Route handling, especially when something changes between the proxy's incoming and outgoing sides: transport protocol switching, multi-homed proxies, IPv4 to IPv6 changes. Earlier documents ([RFC3486], RFC 3608 and an IPv6 transition draft) each recommended double Record-Routing for their own use case, but none gave a general answer, and the description in RFC 3261 never changed. This RFC collects the guidance in one place and also follows up a bug entry (Bug 664) that asked for the language to cover every case of different interfaces on each side, including IPv4 on one side and IPv6 on the other.
sections.eli5: People kept getting confused about how a go-between should leave a return address. This paper clears it up in one place.

sections.title: Multi-Homed Proxies
sections.content:
A multi-homed proxy is connected, like a router, to two or more networks, with an interface in each, so traffic comes in one network and goes out a different one. The RFC's example has a proxy P with addresses 192.0.2.65 and 192.0.2.129, a user agent UA1 at 192.0.2.66 and another, UA2, at 192.0.2.130.

UA1 and UA2 may have no IP-level route between them at all, so pinging or traceroute between them can fail. They can still exchange SIP messages because P is a SIP proxy and applies Record-Routing. In most real cases some IP connectivity exists, but the proxy still has to manage two different sides, for example two different IP addresses, or one side using SigComp compression and the other not.
sections.eli5: Two houses on different streets cannot reach each other directly, but a messenger who stands at the corner of both streets can carry notes between them.

sections.title: The Problems in RFC 3261
sections.content:
Two passages of RFC 3261 set the stage. For requests, the Record-Route URI MUST be a SIP or SIPS URI, and it SHOULD NOT contain the transport parameter unless the proxy knows the next downstream element supports that transport. The RFC says this leaves it unclear when a proxy should insert the transport parameter.

For responses, RFC 3261 says a proxy MAY rewrite its own Record-Route value before forwarding the response, which is useful for multi-homed hosts. It also said that if the request arrived over TLS and left over a non-TLS connection, the proxy MUST rewrite the URI to be a SIPS URI. RFC 5630 has since weakened that requirement by removing the second paragraph.

Rewriting and double Record-Routing both apply whenever the proxy changes its IP address, transport protocol or URI scheme between its incoming and outgoing interfaces.
sections.eli5: The old rules said you could fix the return address on the way back, and they were vague about one detail. That vagueness made people disagree.

sections.title: Why Rewriting Is Not Ideal
sections.content:
With Record-Route rewriting, the proxy edits its own Record-Route value in responses. The RFC says this is not the optimal way to handle multi-homed and transport-switching situations, and names two costs.

  • The route set seen by the caller differs from the one seen by the callee. The callee cannot sign the route set because the proxy edits it in the response, so end-to-end protection of the route set cannot be supported.
  • The proxy needs special multi-homed logic. It computes the output interface on the request and writes it into the URI. On every response it must inspect the Record-Route headers, find the input interface and edit them selectively, which the RFC calls a CPU drag.

The RFC therefore recommends double Record-Routing instead, for all uses of rewriting, including transport protocol switching and multi-homed proxies.
sections.eli5: Changing the return address after the letter is already on its way means the sender and receiver end up holding different copies, and the post office has to check every letter. That is slow and messy.

sections.title: Double Record-Routing
sections.content:
In double Record-Routing the proxy inserts, before any existing Record-Route header, one header whose URI reflects the input interface (including scheme and URI parameters), and a second whose URI reflects the output interface. When the response is processed, nothing needs to be modified. This is completely backward compatible with RFC 3261, and the proxy does no searching or rewriting on responses.

The cost is that the proxy sees later in-dialog requests as a spiral and must keep transactions for it. To avoid that, the proxy can look one extra Route header ahead to see whether the request will spiral through it. Implementers can therefore choose that a proxy MAY remove two Route headers instead of one in the Route Information Preprocessing step of RFC 3261.

The RFC walks through an IPv4 to IPv6 example. Proxy P1 for biloxy.example.com has 192.0.2.254 on its IPv4 interface and 2001:db8::1 on its IPv6 interface. The INVITE it forwards carries two Record-Route headers, the IPv6 one first and the IPv4 one second. UA1 stores them in the opposite order as its route set, so its ACK goes to the IPv4 address first, then to the IPv6 one, and the proxy strips both Route headers before forwarding.

The ordering flips because each user agent builds its route set from the point of view of its own direction, but the proxy never has to edit anything.
sections.eli5: The post office stamps two return addresses on the envelope, one for each door. Nobody has to change anything later, and replies find their way back.

sections.title: The Transport Parameter
sections.content:
RFC 3261 says the Record-Route URI SHOULD NOT contain a transport parameter unless the proxy knows the next element supports it. The RFC says this confused implementers, and proxies inserted a single Record-Route with no transport parameter, which causes trouble.

The worked case is a proxy switching from TCP to UDP. Alice's user agent talks TCP to the proxy, and Bob registered with UDP. The proxy Record-Routes 192.0.2.1 with no transport. Because that is a numeric IP address, the resolution rules of RFC 3263 default to UDP and do no NAPTR lookup, so Alice's later ACK is sent over UDP. Her user agent is not ready to change transport mid-dialog and fails.

For user agents the RFC recommends:

  • Offering a way to force the transport for initial requests SHOULD be avoided, because it bypasses RFC 3263.
  • A user agent that wants a stable transport SHOULD rely on DNS and use a logical name with no transport parameter instead of a numeric IP address.
  • User agents SHOULD be ready to change transport between the initial request and later in-dialog messages.

For proxies, if the transport changes between the incoming and outgoing sides, the proxy SHOULD use double Record-Routing and SHOULD add a transport parameter to each Record-Route URI it inserts. When TLS is used on either side, the URI MUST encode a next hop reached using TLS, either as a SIPS URI or as a URI whose RFC 3263 resolution selects TLS. Proxies MUST NOT use transport=tls, which RFC 3261 deprecated. The advice does not apply when the proxy switched transport only because the UDP request was too large.

Adding the transport parameter is acceptable only if every SIP element that may be on the path of later requests supports that transport. The RFC's example is a proxy P1 switching from UDP to SCTP when the next proxy P2 does not Record-Route: the element downstream of P2 would be asked to reach P1 over SCTP and might not support it. Applying double Record-Routing as soon as the transport changes avoids that. A proxy SHOULD also Record-Route for any multi-homed situation that could affect later requests, such as scheme changes, SigComp, IPv4 and IPv6, or transport changes.
sections.eli5: If the return address does not say how to deliver, the reply goes by the default method, which may not be the one the other side expects. Say the delivery method in the address, but only if everyone along the way can handle it.

sections.title: Conclusion and Security
sections.content:
The conclusion restates the position. Rewriting is a technique that MAY be used. Double Record-Routing is the technique that SHOULD be used. Proxies SHOULD use it for any multi-homed situation that could affect later processing. User agents SHOULD NOT offer options to override the transport for initial requests.

On security, the RFC introduces no new protocol mechanism and so no new concerns, but it asks for more care with existing ones. With double Record-Routing, information about both interfaces reaches each endpoint and any intermediaries, whereas rewriting exposes only the interface closest to each endpoint. If topology hiding or privacy (see RFC 3323) matters, the URIs placed in the headers should be constructed carefully so they expose no more than intended.
sections.eli5: Leaving two return addresses shows both doors of the post office. If you want to keep one door secret, be careful what you write.
